rubric.why: The electron configuration shows that chlorine has seven electrons in its outermost shell.
rubric.description: Gives chlorine’s atomic number and electron configuration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for atomic number 17 and configuration 2,8,7.

rubric.why: Chlorine needs one electron to complete its outer shell, so its valency is one.
rubric.description: Explains why chlorine has valency 1.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that chlorine gains or shares one electron to complete its outer shell.

modelAnswer: Chlorine has atomic number 17, so its electronic configuration is 2,8,7.
It needs one electron to complete its outermost shell; therefore, its valency is 1.

items.followUp: Define any five applications of chemistry.

rubric.why: Physical chemistry describes the physical properties and energy changes of matter.
rubric.description: Defines physical chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: Organic chemistry deals with carbon compounds.
rubric.description: Defines organic chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: Inorganic chemistry studies elements and their compounds, generally excluding most carbon compounds.
rubric.description: Defines inorganic chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: Biochemistry concerns chemical substances and processes in living organisms.
rubric.description: Defines biochemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: Industrial chemistry applies chemistry to large-scale production of chemicals and products.
rubric.description: Defines industrial chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

modelAnswer: Physical chemistry deals with the physical properties of matter and the energy changes involved in chemical reactions.
Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that studies carbon compounds.
Inorganic chemistry deals with the properties and reactions of elements and their compounds, generally excluding most carbon compounds.
Biochemistry studies the chemical substances and processes that occur in living organisms.
Industrial chemistry deals with the manufacture of chemical substances and products on an industrial scale.

items.followUp: Describe how Rutherford discovered the atomic nucleus, including a labeled diagram of his experiment.

rubric.why: Cathode rays were studied in a discharge tube containing gas at low pressure.
rubric.description: Describes the discharge tube and low-pressure gas.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the tube and low-pressure conditions.

rubric.why: A high potential difference was applied between the electrodes.
rubric.description: Identifies the electrodes and high voltage.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct electrode arrangement and high voltage.

rubric.why: The rays originate at the cathode and travel towards the anode.
rubric.description: States the direction of the cathode rays.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction.

rubric.why: The rays caused a fluorescent glow where they struck the glass or screen.
rubric.description: States the observation that revealed the rays.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the fluorescent glow observation.

rubric.why: A labeled diagram makes the apparatus and ray direction clear.
rubric.description: Provides a labeled schematic of the discharge tube.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a diagram showing the cathode, anode, and fluorescent screen or glass, with the ray direction indicated.

modelAnswer: Cathode rays were observed in a glass discharge tube containing gas at very low pressure, with two electrodes connected to a high-voltage source.
The rays originated at the cathode and travelled towards the anode.
A fluorescent glow appeared on the glass wall or screen where the rays struck; this showed the presence of rays travelling through the tube.
Schematic: [Cathode (-)] ---- cathode rays ----> [Anode (+)] ----> [Fluorescent screen / glass glow]
The tube should be drawn as a glass enclosure with the cathode and anode inside, a low-pressure gas label, and a high-voltage source connected to the electrodes.

items.followUp: Explain why sweating cools the body and state two factors that affect the rate of evaporation.

rubric.why: The molecules with greater kinetic energy escape from the liquid first.
rubric.description: Explains which molecules escape during evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the more energetic molecules escape.

rubric.why: The remaining liquid loses energy, lowering its temperature; evaporation also takes heat from the surroundings.
rubric.description: Explains why evaporation produces cooling.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking energy loss or heat absorption to cooling.

rubric.why: Temperature, surface area, wind speed, and humidity affect evaporation rate.
rubric.description: Gives one factor affecting evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid factor and its effect on the rate.

rubric.why: A second factor is required; common factors include temperature, surface area, wind speed, and humidity.
rubric.description: Gives a second factor affecting evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a different valid factor and its effect on the rate.

modelAnswer: During evaporation, the more energetic molecules escape from the surface of the liquid.
The molecules left behind have lower average kinetic energy, so the liquid cools; evaporation also takes heat from its surroundings.
A higher temperature increases the rate of evaporation.
A larger surface area increases the rate of evaporation.

items.followUp: Calculate the formula mass of CaCO3. Use Ca = 40 u, C = 12 u, and O = 16 u.

rubric.why: The formula mass is found by adding the atomic masses in the formula, each multiplied by its subscript.
rubric.description: Sets up the formula-mass calculation correctly.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct expression using Na = 23 u, S = 32 u, and O = 16 u.

rubric.why: The sum of the atomic masses is 142 u.
rubric.description: Gives the formula mass with unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct final answer and unit.

modelAnswer: Given: Na = 23 u, S = 32 u, O = 16 u.
Formula mass of Na2SO4 = 2(Na) + 1(S) + 4(O).
Substitution: = 2(23 u) + 32 u + 4(16 u).
Formula mass of Na2SO4 = 142 u.

items.followUp: Define a mole and state how many molecules are present in 2 mol of CO2.

rubric.why: Avogadro’s number is the number of particles in one mole, approximately 6.02 × 10^23.
rubric.description: Defines Avogadro’s number.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the value and its meaning as particles per mole.

rubric.why: An example applies the number to a specific mole quantity of a substance.
rubric.description: Gives one valid example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an example correctly relating one mole to Avogadro’s number of particles.

modelAnswer: Avogadro’s number is the number of particles present in one mole of a substance: 6.02 × 10^23 particles mol−1.
For example, 1 mol of water contains 6.02 × 10^23 water molecules.

items.followUp: Compare a proton and an electron by charge and relative mass.

rubric.why: An electron has charge −1, whereas a neutron has no charge.
rubric.description: Compares the charges of an electron and neutron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating both charges.

rubric.why: A neutron has a mass of about 1 u, while an electron is much lighter.
rubric.description: Compares the relative masses of an electron and neutron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly distinguishing their masses.

modelAnswer: An electron has a charge of −1, while a neutron has no charge (0).
An electron has a very small mass, about 1/1836 u; a neutron has a mass of about 1 u.
